title: slo-tiered-fallback-cost-probe-notes
body:
Objective:
Capture a compact experimental sketch comparing three fallback strategies under tiered SLOs and show rough cost vs latency tradeoffs in text/ASCII form. This is a working note (proto) for platform-level fallback policy recommendations for Dedicated and Hosted routing layers.

Background / motivation:
- Motor: customers ask for both strong p99 SLOs and predictable bill-of-materials. Fallbacks (model variants, lower-cost quantized shards, regional fallbacks) reduce outages but shift latency/cost.
- We need an operational rulebook: when to enable aggressive fallback vs slow strictness depending on SLO tier and traffic mix.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Workload: synthetic chat sessions modeled after medium-length assistant (prompt 120 tokens + reply 220 tokens avg).
- Concurrency profile: 200 concurrent sessions (sustained) + 40% microburst (3x baseline peaks for 30s every 10 minutes).
- Models: baseline-large (L1, float16), quantized-small (Q4_0, L2), regional-fallback (same L1 in remote region inc RTT).
- Policies tested:
  * strict-no-fallback (S) — always route to L1, queue or reject when capacity exceeded.
  * soft-degrade (D) — prefer L1, but for queue > 250ms switch to L2 or quantized instance.
  * tiered-fallback (T) — SLO-aware: PRICED tiers (Gold/Silver/Bronze) where Gold uses S until p99 risk > threshold; Silver uses D; Bronze uses aggressive fallback earlier.

Measurements captured (per-policy):
- p50/p90/p99 response latency (ms)
- cost per 1k tokens ($)
- fraction routed to fallback (%)
- drop/reject rate (%)
- session tail amplification (long-run p99/p999 jump)

Raw ASCII table (aggregated results) — note: numbers are rounded, synthetic run 3/5 seeds: 

Policy | p50 ms | p90 ms | p99 ms | cost /1k tok ($) | fallback % | rejects %
-------|--------|--------|--------|------------------|------------|--------
S      |   110  |   190  |   680  |     0.0125       |     2%     |  3.8%  
D      |   120  |   210  |   320  |     0.0108       |    18%     |  0.4%  
T-Gold |   112  |   195  |   410  |     0.0119       |     6%     |  1.1%  
T-Silver|  130  |   240  |   350  |     0.0102       |    22%     |  0.6%  
T-Bronze|  150  |   320  |   380  |     0.0091       |    37%     |  0.0%  

Interpretation notes (quick):
- Strict (S) preserves token-quality (always L1) but shows bad tails and significant rejects during microbursts — p99=680ms, rejects ~3.8%. Cost is highest.
- Soft-degrade (D) dramatically reduces p99 (to 320ms) and rejects, at modest cost savings (14% lower). Fallback % shows that D used fallbacks for 18% of requests — that explains cost delta.
- Tiered policy (T) results are mixed; Gold profile stays close to S in p50/p90 but caps rejects at lower rate by allowing small fallback fraction. Bronze shifts cost aggressively (savings ~27% vs S) while keeping rejects near zero, but median latency suffers.

ASCII mini-visual: p99 vs cost (normalized to S) — each line is policy: bars approximate p99 (left) and cost (right) with scale markers. Lower cost desired, lower p99 desired.
Scale: p99 baseline S=680ms -> normalize to 1.0; cost baseline S=1.0

S      | p99 [####################] 1.00 | cost [####################] 1.00
D      | p99 [###########       ] 0.47 | cost [#############     ] 0.86
T-Gold | p99 [###########  ] 0.60 | cost [################  ] 0.95
T-Silv | p99 [########### ] 0.51 | cost [###########      ] 0.82
T-Brnz | p99 [#########    ] 0.56 | cost [########         ] 0.73

Notes on what drives differences:
- Fallback choice: switching to quantized L2 saves kernel time and memory bandwidth, lowering token cost. But for certain prompts (long context), quantization introduces decode variance causing slight latency jitter.
- Queueing vs immediate fallback: policies that wait (D) still take a small penalty for queued tokens but avoid rejects — overall better p99/cost balance.
- Distance/regional fallbacks add RTT penalty; those variants had p90 increase but were cheaper when compute in remote zone has lower unit cost. Should treat regional fallback as last resort.

Microbench labels (sample) — session cohort slice: 
- Cohort A (short-turn prompts, 60 tokens replies): D performs best (low p99, modest fallback).
- Cohort B (long-turn, 600 token replies): D shows more variance when fallback triggers (quantized mismatch), T-Gold preferred for minimal quality loss.

Open questions / TODOs (explicit):
- Quality regression analysis: we only measured latency/cost. Need a quality delta metric (log-prob or human eval) for fallback output vs baseline L1. How much quality loss acceptable per tier? (action: @Priya to run llm-eval harness PLAT-1463).
- Auto-threshold calibration: D uses a 250ms queue threshold. That number was toy. We should sweep 100-400ms and measure cost delta curve. (action: @Ethan to run param sweep).
- Admission control interaction: how do tenant-level burst budgets interact with tiered-fallback? Need to simulate multi-tenant attribution to see starvation cases.
- Observability hooks: add metric labels for fallback.reason and fallback.selected_variant to Console traces. Also add SLO-tier histograms.

Quick recommendations (proto):
1) Default hosted API: adopt soft-degrade (D) as platform default for public low-latency products. It reduces p99 >2x vs strict while saving ~14% cost.
2) Offer tiered policy per-customer: expose Gold/Silver/Bronze knobs. Default mapping: Gold->strict with small fallback allowance, Silver->soft-degrade, Bronze->aggressive. Provide estimated cost % delta in Console (approx numbers shown).
3) Gate regional fallbacks behind a flag; prefer quantized local fallback first.

Short checklist to ship next experiment: 
- [ ] run quality-eval on 1k prompts across cohorts A/B for L1 vs L2 (lead: Priya, due 2028-11-16)
- [ ] sweep queue threshold at 100/200/300/400ms (lead: Ethan, due 2028-11-20)
- [ ] instrument fallback labels in Console (owner: Jordan, due 2028-11-12)
- [ ] create Confluence summary + decision record (owner: Marisol, linked PF-5543)

Notes-to-self / rough scribbles:
- early impression: strict-only is rarely optimal for bursty SaaS apps; tails cost more in business terms (P99 outages cause downstream UI retries and session churn).
- possible UX: let customers pick "latency-first" vs "cost-first" and map to policy automatically. Map to price multiplier in billing UI.

References / linked quick reads:
- PF-5543 (design sketch for fallback routing)
- PLAT-1458 (ticket for tiered SLO routing)

Any immediate objections or angles I missed? Add below and I'll fold into the next run notes.

-- Marisol R. (working draft, please mark comments inline)
